headline: This $1,800 Handheld Gaming PC Is Amazing But Still Not Worth Buying

levels.label: Grade 3-4
levels.summary: A handheld gaming PC is like a mix between a laptop and a video game controller. You can play big computer games while holding it in your hands, like a Nintendo Switch. A reviewer tested a new one called the MSI Claw EX. It has a strong computer chip inside, so games look sharper and run smoother than on other similar devices. Its battery also lasts a long time, and it can go to sleep and wake back up without problems, which other similar gadgets often struggle with. But there are two big problems. First, it costs $1,800, which is a huge amount of money for a handheld device. Second, sometimes the games glitch, freeze, or even make the whole device stop working. The reviewer loves testing it and uses it more than any other handheld he owns. But he says most people should not buy it yet, because it is too expensive and not perfectly reliable. It shows what future handhelds might be like, but it is not quite ready for regular shoppers.

levels.label: Grade 5-6
levels.summary: Handheld gaming PCs are small, portable devices that let you play full computer games anywhere, similar to a Nintendo Switch but more powerful. A tech reviewer at The Verge tested a new one called the MSI Claw EX, which uses a brand-new Intel computer chip. He says it is the most powerful and longest-lasting handheld he has tested, and it is also the first Windows-based handheld that can reliably go to sleep and wake up again, like a smartphone. Other Windows handhelds often struggle with that simple task. In his tests, the Claw EX ran demanding video games about 40% faster than a similar competitor, the Xbox Ally X. It also used less battery power to get the same smooth performance, meaning gamers can play longer before recharging. However, the device is far from perfect. Some games glitched, showed broken graphics, or even froze the whole system because the newer Intel chip isn't fully supported yet by all games. The reviewer also ran into annoying Windows software problems, like games not showing on screen properly. On top of all that, this handheld costs a shocking $1,800, and it's hard to even find one for sale. Because of the high price and the software bugs, the reviewer says this device proves handheld gaming PCs are getting much better, but he still would not recommend that people actually buy this particular model right now.

levels.label: Grade 7-8
levels.summary: Handheld gaming PCs are portable devices, similar to a Nintendo Switch, that let players run full PC video games while holding a controller-shaped device. The Verge's reviewer tested MSI's newest model, the Claw 8 EX AI Plus, which uses a brand-new Intel processor chip called Panther Lake. He calls it a huge step forward for the category because it solves two problems that have plagued Windows-based handhelds: performance and reliable sleep mode. Unlike other Windows handhelds, this one can be put to sleep and later woken up instantly, exactly where you left off, similar to how the popular Steam Deck already works. It can even sit unused for days without losing much battery charge. In benchmark tests, the Claw EX ran demanding games roughly 40% faster than a similar competitor, the Xbox Ally X, and could hit the same performance using noticeably less power, which stretches battery life longer. In one battery test playing a simple card game, adjusting a few settings let it run for 12 hours straight. However, the reviewer found real problems too. Because the Intel chip is brand new, some games have driver issues — meaning the software that connects the game to the hardware isn't fully finished. This caused graphical glitches, missing visual effects, stuttering, and in one case a total system freeze during gameplay. Performance also dropped sharply once the battery fell below 15%. Beyond the hardware, typical Windows annoyances remained, such as games launching invisibly in the background or a confusing permissions error blocking the settings menu. Perhaps the biggest issue, though, is the price: $1,800, which is far more than most gaming laptops, let alone handhelds. It's also hard to actually buy one, since supply is limited. Because of the high cost and unfinished software, the reviewer concludes that while the Claw EX proves handheld PCs can finally deliver strong performance and battery life together, this specific product isn't practical for most people to purchase right now — it's more of a preview of what's coming next.

levels.label: Grade 9-10
levels.summary: In the fast-growing world of handheld gaming PCs — small, portable devices that run full computer games while you hold them like a controller — The Verge's reviewer says MSI's new Claw 8 EX AI Plus is the biggest leap forward since Valve's Steam Deck helped launch the category. The reason is a brand-new Intel processor called Panther Lake. It delivers noticeably better graphics performance, roughly 40% faster than a comparable competitor, the Xbox Ally X, while also using less energy to hit the same frame rates. That efficiency translates into meaningfully longer battery life, something handheld PC owners have long complained about. Just as importantly, the Claw EX solves a persistent annoyance with Windows-based handhelds: unreliable sleep mode. Previously, putting these devices to sleep and later waking them up often caused crashes or lost progress. The Claw EX can sleep for days and wake instantly with your game exactly where you left it, matching a feature Steam Deck users have enjoyed for years. Despite these advances, the reviewer stops short of recommending it. Because the Intel chip is so new, many games' graphics drivers — the software translating game code into what you see on screen — haven't caught up yet. This caused visual glitches, missing special effects, stuttering, and in at least one case, a complete system freeze during gameplay. Performance would also unexpectedly drop when the battery dipped below 15%, and it wouldn't fully recover even after plugging the device back in. Old-fashioned Windows quirks persisted too: games sometimes launched invisibly in the background, driver updates weren't announced automatically, and at one point the device's own settings menu locked the reviewer out, incorrectly claiming he lacked administrator permission. Then there's the price. At $1,800, the Claw EX costs roughly double what many competing handhelds sell for, and supply is so limited that finding one to buy may be difficult even for people willing to pay. Combining a high price with unresolved software bugs, the reviewer frames this device as a milestone worth admiring rather than a purchase worth making — proof that powerful, long-lasting, reliably sleeping Windows handhelds are finally possible, but not yet ready for everyday buyers who need something that simply works out of the box.

levels.label: Grade 11+
levels.summary: Handheld gaming PCs occupy a growing niche between smartphones, consoles, and laptops: compact devices that run full PC game libraries while fitting in two hands, popularized by Valve's Steam Deck. The Verge's reviewer argues that MSI's newest entry, the Claw 8 EX AI Plus, represents the category's most significant advancement since that original Steam Deck, thanks largely to Intel's new Panther Lake processor architecture. In controlled benchmarks across multiple demanding titles, the Claw EX outperformed a leading rival, the Xbox Ally X, by roughly 40% at matched settings, while simultaneously requiring less electrical power to achieve equivalent frame rates. That power efficiency is significant because it directly extends battery life — a persistent weakness of portable PC gaming compared to dedicated consoles. Perhaps more notably, the Claw EX addresses a longstanding software failure of Windows-based handhelds: unreliable sleep and resume functionality. Historically, closing the lid or pressing the power button on these devices, rather than fully shutting down, has risked crashes, corrupted saves, or games failing to resume properly. The Claw EX instead mimics smartphone-like sleep behavior, preserving battery charge for days and resuming exactly where the player left off — a baseline expectation for consumer electronics that Windows PC handhelds have struggled for years to meet. Despite these genuine advances, the reviewer withholds a recommendation, and his reasoning illustrates a broader tension in adopting brand-new hardware. Because Panther Lake is a newly released chip, many game developers' graphics drivers — the intermediary software translating a game's rendering instructions into what actually appears on screen — haven't yet been optimized for it. The consequences ranged from cosmetic issues, like corrupted particle effects and missing environmental details, to functional failures, including stuttering, refusal to maintain selected power settings, and at least one full system freeze mid-gameplay. Battery-related performance also degraded unpredictably below 15% charge and didn't reliably recover even after recharging. Layered atop these hardware-specific issues are familiar Windows-on-handheld frustrations: games silently launching in windowed mode behind a black screen, absent notifications for critical driver updates, and an erroneous permissions error that temporarily locked the reviewer out of his own settings menu. Finally, and most decisively for ordinary consumers, the device costs $1,800 — a price point closer to premium gaming laptops than typical handhelds — while remaining difficult to actually purchase due to limited stock. The reviewer's verdict captures a common pattern in cutting-edge consumer technology: a device can be an important technical milestone, demonstrating what's newly possible, while still being an impractical purchase for most people due to unresolved bugs, immature software support, and pricing that outpaces its real-world reliability.

questions: If a cool new gadget is expensive and still has bugs, would you rather buy it early or wait for it to improve? Why?
How do you think it feels for a company to release a product that's impressive but not perfect — and what responsibility do they have to fix problems after it's sold?
Battery life and performance are often trade-offs in technology we use every day, like phones and laptops. How does that trade-off affect your own choices when picking a device?
